comment.value:
The paper introduces a large-scale text-to-query dataset specifically designed for electronic health records. This dataset is among the first to include multiple languages for data-centric code generation tasks. This makes this a promising dataset that may become quite impactful.

That said, I'd recommend that the authors further improve the paper:
* From the perspective of EHRs and data models, more clear evidence is needed to justify the necessity of multiple data models.
* Compared to existing datasets, the queries seem overly simple, lacking multi-hop complexity and real-world applicability.
* The total number of synthetic patient samples was not mentioned (or hard to find) in the paper. It is very vital because it decides how hard the patient search tasks can be.
* It is vital but not mentioned in the data that, in real-world cases, patient data may store records that were not well-standardized. That is why, in practice, researchers need to define a concept set for the entity mentioned in the query. That concept set can be very broad and cover many entities defined in varied medical ontologies. Is it unclear if this paper considered this when building the synthetic patient data?

In all, this dataset is likely to stimulate important healthcare applications, and the remaining issues can likely be overcome in the next version of the paper and dataset.

Thank you for considering our rebuttal and raising your score. We are looking forward to improving our paper based on your and the other reviewers' very constructive comments in the revision of our paper.

Thank you for the detailed explanations and thoughtful consideration of the review. Most of my concerns have been addressed, prompting me to raise my score. I believe this dataset will be valuable for evaluating Text-to-Query research across various database models with their corresponding syntax. 

However, it has limitations in the medical domain due to the restricted semantic space of the queries compared to previous medical Text-to-Query benchmarks. As evidenced in the attached PDF materials, this dataset shows significantly lower numbers of tokens, keywords, joins/traversals, and nesting depths compared to MIMICSQL and EHRSQL, particularly when comparing the complexity of the semantic space using the same syntax (SQL). Consequently, the SQL queries are relatively simple, with the corresponding natural language utterances typically traversing only a few tables through basic pathways. I understand that standard-based and privacy-preserving considerations would be effective for populating more queries by using constructed templates. However, without consideration of diverse information-seeking needs, it's hard to make an impact on real-world health use cases.

**Q1:**
We generated 100 patients using the synthetic data generation framework from Synthea. The reason for choosing 100 patients is mainly due to the query performance implications of databases such as GraphDB (used for RDF). As we have experienced in previous projects with larger Synthea datasets, the query execution time could exceed multiple minutes per query on standard hardware, if there is a vast amount of data in the graph database. It is important to note that the Synthea data usually has a large number of observations, encounter descriptions, and claim transactions per patient. However, given that our synthetic data generation framework is parameterizable, we can easily extend its size to a larger patient population. We can consider to additionally release a SM3-Text-to-QueryLarge besides the standard version of our benchmark. In its current version we ensure that users can execute the benchmark on common hardware in a reasonable time and thus make it more accessible.

**Q2:**
Our benchmark is synthetically generated and hence entity matching is not an issue. However, there are many well-established entity matching algorithms that can be used in case datasets are not standardized such as:

Fernando de Meer Pardo, Claude Lehmann, Dennis Gehrig, Andrea Nagy, Stefano Nicoli, Branka Hadji Misheva, Martin Braschler, Kurt Stockinger: GraLMatch: Matching Groups of Entities with Graphs and Language Models. EDBT 2025: 1-12

Jonathan Fürst, Mauricio Fadel Argerich, Bin Cheng: VersaMatch: Ontology Matching with Weak Supervision. Proc. VLDB Endow. 16(6): 1305-1318 (2023)

Ursin Brunner, Kurt Stockinger: Entity Matching with Transformer Architectures - A Step Forward in Data Integration. EDBT 2020: 463-473 

It can be a good idea to consider an extension to our current benchmark in which the data is purposely made noisy through variations in entity names and spelling mistakes. This could test the robustness of current Text-to-Query approaches.

**Additional feedback:**

1. The rationale for testing LLMs without schema is to perform ablation studies. We wanted to show the impact of using and not-using the schema. Another reason is that for RDF graph databases (unlike for relational databases), the schema is not always available or required to enable more flexible data integration. Hence, RDF graph databases are typically more challenging for LLMs due to missing, incomplete or contradictory schema descriptions - as is often the case for the RDF databases DBPedia.

2. See also answer Q1 to Reviewer 31NM. 
It is correct that the relational model and SQL is the most common architecture for EHRs. However, we are seeing increasingly that EHRs are connected with other data sources and thus a more flexible cross-silo model and query language is needed. Here the graph model is in fact already used for this purpose. For example, AICCELERATE (https://aiccelerate.eu), a recent large-scale European pilot project on digital hospitals, uses the graph model. Also in the context of our current Digital Health Zurich project (https://www.dizh.uzh.ch/en/2022/07/07/zurich-applied-digital-health-center-2), the University Hospital Balgrist is deploying EHR prototypes with other data models.
Moreover, the use of RDF graph databases with SPARQL as the main query language is widely used in the life science community with medicine catching up [1]. We will point out these pieces of evidence in a revision of our paper to better motivate the construction of our dataset. 

3. See also answer in Q1. We are using Synthea to create synthetic patient data. Synthea uses real demographic data to inform its population generation. This helps ensure that the synthetic population reflects realistic distributions of various demographic factors. For our benchmark we are using its default configuration (https://github.com/synthetichealth/synthea/blob/master/src/main/resources/synthea.properties), which is based on data from the U.S. Census Bureau. With our benchmark, we also release all code and instructions necessary to create synthetic patient data and Text/Query pairs for individual usage requirements (e.g., data for different populations).
We made sure that the template queries are diverse enough by creating them for all SNOMED classes. In the future we will extend our templates based on further feedback from our medical partners. 

[1] Sima, A. C.,et al.. (2022). Bio-SODA UX: enabling natural language question answering over knowledge graphs with user disambiguation. Distributed and Parallel Databases, 40(2), 409-440.

Thank you for the positive review and suggestions. Please find our responses below.

**Q1:**
We will improve the introduction with an overview figure as suggested and provide more medical background information about electronic health records.
Healthcare is the general term we use for the application field. We need to distinguish between medical research and clinical practice. The focus of medical research is to study new treatments, new medications or new digital technologies in the field of healthcare. Clinical practice refers to the applications of best practices derived from medical research. Our focus is to help accelerate medical research by enabling healthcare professionals to analyze large amounts of heterogeneous datasets intuitively without being an expert in computer science or query languages.

**Q2:**
In our current benchmark we use synthetic data which does not reveal any specific private data. Moreover, the benchmark corresponds with domain knowledge since it adheres to best practices in medical data modeling. Enhancing the benchmark with augmented data can be achieved in specific hospitals or settings, where the data scientists have the right to work with the data. Depending on the setting of the hospital, the data can be further anonymized. In addition, hospitals can use the Generic Module Frameworks https://github.com/synthetichealth/synthea/wiki/Generic-Module-Framework to augment our benchmark data set with hospital-specif data.

**Q3:**
Even though RDF and the SPARQL query language have been widely used in life sciences and the semantic web community, the usage in industrial settings is still rather limited. There are considerably fewer resources available for SPARQL than for SQL, which in turn is widely used in industry. Hence, the LLMs struggle particularly with SPARQL due to the low number of resources and the more complex nature of SPARQL compared to SQL (see also overall rebuttal comments where we compare our results to the number of related Stackoverflow posts). 

**Q4:**
The splitting of the dataset in train, dev and test was done randomly. The possibility of the sampled data not being representative in any of the respective parts was mitigated by reviewing  the unsplit data. Through the  Kolmogorov-Smirnov test and a correlation heat map it could be shown that the sampled data indeed originated from the base question templates and has a representative distribution of these questions.

rebuttal.value:
**Q1:**
You are correct that the relational model and SQL is the most common architecture for EHRs. However, we are seeing increasingly that EHRs are connected with other data sources and a more flexible cross-silo model and query language is needed. Here the graph model is in fact already used for this purpose. E.g., in AICCELERATE (https://aiccelerate.eu), a recent large-scale European pilot project on digital hospitals. Also the University Hospital Balgrist is deploying EHR prototypes with other data models in our current Digital Health Zurich project.
Moreover, RDF graph databases with SPARQL as the main query language are widely used in life science with medicine catching up [1].

**Q2:**
The dataset was created over the period of more than a year based on a project with health professionals from two university hospitals, medical doctors, nurses, data scientists and computer scientists who have been working in the respective fields for 5+ years. Hence, the team has expert knowledge both in medicine and life sciences as well as in database design, query languages and building benchmark datasets in academic and industrial settings.
We constructed the question templates to cover all SNOMED CT entities. The database queries were mainly written by two undergraduate and one PhD student with a CS and database background and verified by two faculty members. 

**Q3:**
We have computed the query statistics used in our paper also for EHRSQL and MIMICSQL (**see Table 1 in the rebuttal attachement**). As the reviewer rightly pointed out, EHRSQL and MIMICSQL contain more difficult SQL queries (e.g., temporal). However, the strength of our dataset lies in its cross-model aspect, adding Cypher, MQL and SPARQL. As can be seen in Table 1, our MQL and SPARQL queries are of similar complexity in terms of number of tokens. However, SPARQL contains more joins/traversals than existing benchmarks, while MQL contains more nesting. Our dataset will be a useful resource not only to the medical domain, but to AI and NLP researchers working on Text-to-Query in general.

**Q4:**
As we have shown in ScienceBenchmark [2], T5 is not competitive any more for Text-to-SQL for complex databases. Additionally, it requires high GPU usage to fine-tune to a new dataset or even new query language. Previously we fine-tuned a T5 model for a Text-to-SQL task with the Spider dataset (7K training pairs) and it required a A100 GPU for 44 days. We would need to fine-tune four T5 models for the current paper (four query languages) which would require approx. 25 weeks of fine-tuning. Hence, we only focused on modern large language models with ICL. However, as suggested, we can report results for two more experiments:

**1. Simple baseline based on predicting most frequent labels.**

The most frequent labels in the train set are the non-answerable questions (201 counts). If we apply a predictor with this most frequent label to test, which contains 55 non-answerable questions out of 2000, we achieve an execution accuracy of 55/2000 = 2.75%.

***2. More advanced ICL based on BM25-based few-shot selection (see Table 2 in pdf)***

We implement a similarity based approach using a BM25 retriever that, on a per question basis, retrieves the five most similar question-query pairs from the training data. We use these question pairs as few-shot examples instead of the fixed few-shots used before. We use the w/ schema prompt with GPT-3.5. This greatly improves results to up to 88.55% for SQL, which is in line with related results in EHRXQA [3].
EHRXQA is based on EHRSQL, while adding a Visual Question Answering (VQA) task to it. However, the authors also partially evaluate the performance of table-related queries (i.e., conventional Text-to-SQL). As an end-to-end comparison, they achieve an execution accuracy of 92.9%, an improvement by 62.9 points from their fixed-shot strategy. This is consistent with our results, where SQL execution accuracy improves by 32.13 points to 88.55%. However, we can also see that even with a state-of-the-art ICL method, SPARQL, Cypher, and MQL cannot reach the same performance as SQL (MQL has the highest score with 78.70%). This indicates the need for more research, such as developing better ICL methods and potentially schema encodings. Overall, it reinforces the motivation and strengthens the necessity of our work in terms of creating a new multi-model Text-to-Query benchmark to work on these problems and to extend the research scope from "Text-to-SQL" to multi-model "Text-to-Query".

**Answers to additional feedback:**
1. We are happy to improve Table 1 based on your feedback. We feel that the separate columns are necessary to emphasize the different data models covered by our benchmark. 
2. We had 10 unanswerable medical questions and 5 unanswerable non-medical questions in the 408 templates.
3. Output of Synthea: Based on the specified CSV output, one CSV file per class is generated in the simulation. Default configurations create the medical records of 100 living patients and 10 dead patients. All data is used for the creation of the different databases, while patient expenses and payer transitions are excluded from the benchmark dataset. This design choice is made because they are mainly used to map between classes.

[1] Sima, A. C.,et al.. (2022). Bio-SODA UX: enabling natural language question answering over knowledge graphs with user disambiguation. Distributed and Parallel Databases, 40(2), 409-440.

[2] Zhang, Y., Deriu, J., Katsogiannis-Meimarakis, G., Kosten, C., Koutrika, G., & Stockinger, K. (2023). ScienceBenchmark: A Complex Real-World Benchmark for Evaluating Natural Language to SQL Systems. Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment, 17(4), 685-698.

[3] Bae, S., Kyung, D., Ryu, J., Cho, E., Lee, G., Kweon, S., ... & Choi, E. (2024). Ehrxqa: A multi-modal question answering dataset for electronic health records with chest x-ray images. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 36.

rebuttal.value:
We thank all the reviewers for their constructive comments and have responded individually to them. Overall we would like to emphasize again that the strength of our benchmark is the coverage of three important database models (relational, graph, document) with four query languages (SQL, SPARQL, MQL, Cypher). *Currently, there exists no such dataset and benchmark in and outside the medical domain.*
Regarding the requests of *Reviewer gjFK24* and *Reviewer BzGp23* for a better explanation/failure analysis with regards to different database models and query languages, we can add the following further observations:

**1. Implicit LLM Knowledge vs Query Language**   
LLMs contain a vastly different level of knowledge of the different query languages based on their training data. A large ressource of such training data has been Stackoverflow. When we search Stackoverflow for tags (indicated with  []) related to our four query languages, we get the following numbers (15.08.2024):
- [SQL]: 673K posts
- [SPARQL]: 6K posts
- [MongoDB] [MQL]: 176K posts
- [Cypher] [Neo4J]: 33K posts

Relating the size of the posts to our “w/ schema 0-shot” results (we want to leave the impact of few-shots ICL out of this), we see that SQL performs best (best model: 47.5% ), Cypher and MQL perform average (best models: 35.5% and 23%), while SPARQL performs worst (best model: 3.3%). These results correlate to the post frequency on Stackoverflow, with the exception that MQL is underperforming Cypher. We suspect that this has to do with the fact that Cypher queries contain much fewer number of tokens and language keywords than MQL (only 25% of tokens and 50% of keywords, see Figure 2 in the main paper).

**2. LLM ICL Capabilities vs Query Languages**   
When adding fixed few-shot in-context learning (ICL) to the prompt, we can observe that SPARQL benefits most from it, improving its performance 10-fold. Cypher and MQL nearly doubled in performance. For SQL, the random, fixed few-shots provide only a much smaller improvement. This indicates again that the model is already capable in the SQL query language, whereas for SPARQL (and to a smaller extend Cypher and MQL), the model is truly benefiting from ICL by learning how to formulate more correct queries from the provided fixed few-shot examples (even though the examples might not directly be related to the asked question).

We will further document these observations and the ones pointed out in the individual rebuttals in the revision of our paper.

summary_and_contributions.value: This work presents a Text-to-Query benchmark, particularly in the medical domain, spanning three core database models (relational, graph, document) and four query languages (SQL, SPARQL, Cypher, MQL). All samples share the same synthetic patient data, which incorporates a commonly used medical ontology (i.e., SNOMED-CT), potentially facilitating connections between this benchmark and real-world applications. The paper also contributes 408 base question templates that can be combined with SNOMED-CT entities, ultimately resulting in a total of 10,000 samples for each query language (therefore, a total of 40,000 samples in the dataset). Evaluation results vary across different experimental settings, including four LLMs with different prompting techniques and four query languages. Unsurprisingly, the benchmark achieves its best scores with an increased number of few-shot examples, more advanced LLMs, the inclusion of schema information, and the use of the most widely recognized query language syntax.

review.value:
Pros:
- The database and dataset are standards-based and privacy-preserving, allowing them to be generated in a simulated manner.
- The consideration of diverse database models and query syntax provides a valuable resource for the database and AI community.

Cons:
- From the perspective of EHRs and data models, more clear evidence is needed to justify the necessity of multiple data models.
- Compared to existing datasets, the queries seem overly simple, lacking multi-hop complexity and real-world applicability.
- There are no reference points, such as simple baselines (e.g., predicting frequent labels) or fine-tuned baselines using models like T5, which could potentially achieve state-of-the-art performance for each task, making it difficult to gauge the benchmark's difficulty.
- There is a lack of detailed scientific findings/analyses, through comprehensible failure analysis, explaining why different syntax queries, given the same semantic query, vary in difficulty (some are harsh; some are easy).

strengths.value: Please refer to the "Pros" part in the above "Review" section.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
- Q1: Most related research in the healthcare domain, such as MIMICSQL or EHRSQL, assumes that EHRs are retrieved from a relational database using SQL syntax. However, this work targets EHRs with multiple data models, including graph and document models. Given that EHRs are typically stored in relational databases, is there explicit evidence or are there cases demonstrating the necessity of exploring versatile data models or evaluating other query syntaxes? What are the possibilities and pros/cons of deploying real EHRs using different data models?

- Q2: For the dataset construction process, a detailed explanation would be helpful. Who were the experts or annotators involved in creating this dataset? How many days were spent on this process? What expertise did they have, particularly regarding databases and EHRs? Were there any specific annotation or labeling protocols or criteria used?

- Q3: Considering the information from the SQL part (tokens, keywords, joins/traversals/nesting depth) in Figure 2, although the template size looks large (408 templates), the queries appear simple. In other words, the entire semantic space is not complex and might not be helpful for complex real-world queries (such as survival rate, temporal comparative queries in EHRSQL). For the current version, is there any comparison of template queries (e.g., the number of joins, tables per query) in other datasets such as MIMICSQL and EHRSQL?

- Q4: For the experimental part, could you provide reference points, such as simple baselines (e.g., predicting frequent labels) or more powerful ICL methods or fine-tuned baselines using models like T5, which could potentially achieve state-of-the-art performance for each task, to help gauge the benchmark's difficulty?

correctness.value: Yes, the claims made in the paper appear to be correct, and the dataset seems to be constructed in a sound manner.

clarity.value: Yes, the paper is generally well-written.

relation_to_prior_work.value: Yes, the paper discusses this in Section 2 (L83-L118) and Section 4 (L207-L213).

- Line 180: How many non-answerable medical and non-medical questions are there among the 408 template questions? Please specify them.
- Line 144: Where can I find the details about the “Synthea output”?

summary_and_contributions.value:
1. The paper introduces a large-scale text-to-query dataset specifically designed for electronic health records.
2. This dataset is among the first to include multiple languages for data-centric code generation tasks.
3. The authors detail methods to expand the dataset using templates, which is particularly beneficial for domains like healthcare that handle private and scarce data.
4. The experimental setup is thorough, including multiple families of large language models (LLMs), both open-sourced and proprietary.

review.value:
strong points:

1. Collecting a healthcare dataset is challenging; the authors provide a large-scale dataset to inspire further research and development of effective applications in this domain, demonstrating significant social impact.
2. The data augmentation methods presented are highly useful for specific, data-scarce domains.
3. This paper is the first I have encountered that offers comprehensive database settings and language coverage for realistic applications.
4. The experiments are insightful and thorough. Notably, Figure 4 helps readers identify the weaknesses of their LLM models and provides a foundation for improvement.

2. The data augmentation methods presented are highly useful for specific, data-scarce domains.
3. This paper is the first I have encountered that offers comprehensive database settings and language coverage for realistic applications.
4. The experiments are insightful and thorough. Notably, Figure 4 helps readers identify the weaknesses of their LLM models and provides a foundation for improvement.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
1. The presentations should be refined:
a. Authors didn't provide an overview or teaser picture in the introduction, which is a little hard for readers, especially those with diverse backgrounds to follow and get the pain point. Please consider configuring one.
b. Authors could consider introducing more background knowledge about electronic health care since this is a dataset based on specific domains. To me, it's hard to differentiate the meanings between "healthcare", and "clinic", could authors clarify these, and which is the focus of this paper? It would be better to understand this paper.
c. In Section 5.1, it's a little weird to see two citation formats.
2. The core 408 sets were collected with privacy issues resolved, which is valuable. However, it is unclear how privacy is ensured with the augmented data. If the new data is synthetic, does it conform to domain knowledge and not map to real individuals? This should be discussed, especially since the augmented data is used for LLM evaluation.
3. It would be helpful if the authors identified which language poses the greatest challenge for LLMs and provided observations or hypotheses regarding this. Is it due to the language's complexity or its low-resource nature? A case study illustrating these points would be beneficial.
4. In Section 4, the authors mention splitting the data into train, dev, and test sets. What strategy was used for this split? Was it random, or were out-of-distribution (OOD) problems considered? Clarifying this would provide better insight into the robustness of the experimental setup.

summary_and_contributions.value: This paper proposed a question-to-query dataset for multi-model EHR databases, including relational databases, document stores, and graph databases. The dataset contains 10K question-query pairs for each model, yielding a total number of 40K samples. Based on this dataset, the authors evaluated closed and open-sourced LLMs in the question-to-query tasks via in-context learning. On this dataset, it was found that most existing LLMs obtain relatively low accuracy, so there lies significant room for future improvement.

review.value:
**Pros**

- This paper covers a set of database models that may store patient records in EHR, which sets a comprehensive evaluation of existing LLMs in question-to-query tasks in medicine.

- It is built based on synthetic patient data; hence, it reduces the barrier for future research to keep working on this venue.

- The results were analyzed in-depth to reflect the performance of LLMs across different question types, which is valuable and provides insights for future research to improve.

**Cons**

- The total number of synthetic patient samples was not mentioned (or hard to find) in the paper. It is very vital because it decides how hard the patient search tasks can be. 

- It is vital but not mentioned in the data that, in real-world cases, patient data may store records that were not well-standardized. That is why, in practice, researchers need to define a concept set for the entity mentioned in the query. That concept set can be very broad and cover many entities defined in varied medical ontologies. Is it unclear if this paper considered this when building the synthetic patient data?

flag_for_ethics_review.value: 2: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

additional_feedback.value:
1. Table 2. What's the rationale for testing models without the schema? In this case, I guess there is a minor chance LLMs can generate the right query unless the database schema is well-known or in some standard format, such as OMOP. Can you clarify more on that?

2. In which cases are EHRs stored in graph databases and document databases? As far as I know, most real-world data are stored in relational databases, which is why most previous works generated SQL for EHR databases. 


3. How many synthetic patients have you generated for testing? How do you make sure the patient data are diverse enough?

title.value: SM3-Text-to-Query: Synthetic Multi-Model Medical Text-to-Query Benchmark

TLDR.value: SM3-Text-to-Query is a new multi-model medical Text-to-Query Benchmark for SQL, SPARQL, Cypher and MongoDB Query Language (MQL)

abstract.value:
Electronic health records (EHRs) are stored in various database systems with different database models on heterogeneous storage architectures, such as relational databases, document stores, or graph databases. These different database models have a big impact on query complexity and performance. While this has been a known fact in database research, its implications for the growing number of Text-to-Query systems have surprisingly not been investigated so far.
In this paper, we present SM3-Text-to-Query, the first multi-model medical Text-to-Query benchmark based on synthetic patient data from Synthea, following the SNOMED-CT taxonomy---a widely used knowledge graph ontology covering medical terminology. SM3-Text-to-Query provides data representations for relational databases (PostgreSQL), document stores (MongoDB), and graph databases (Neo4j and GraphDB (RDF)), allowing the evaluation across four popular query languages, namely SQL, MQL, Cypher, and SPARQL.
We systematically and manually develop 408 template questions, which we augment to construct a benchmark of 10K diverse natural language question/query pairs for these four query languages (40K pairs overall). On our dataset, we evaluate several common in-context-learning (ICL) approaches for a set of representative closed and open-source LLMs.
Our evaluation sheds light on the trade-offs between database models and query languages for different ICL strategies and LLMs. Last,
SM3-Text-to-Query is easily extendable to additional query languages or real, standard-based patient databases.

dateprocesses.script:
def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']
    venue_name = domain.content['title']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.utcnow())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.utcnow().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
